findings.suggestion: Add HostCanonicalisationTest.aNonAsciiHostIsCanonicalisedToItsPunycodeForm: assert normalize("bücher.example.com") equals Optional.of("xn--bcher-kva.example.com"), that the result is all-ASCII, that it is idempotent (normalising the punycode form again does not move it), and that a non-ASCII host IDN.toASCII rejects answers Optional.empty() rather than the input.
findings.summary: The IDN/punycode step of HostNormalizer (step 4 of the frozen contract, HostNormalizer.java:173-179) has no test at any level. Every other row of the worked table is pinned - trailing dots, case, all four numeric forms, octal, out-of-range, empty labels, IPv6, idempotence, no-label-removal - but no test passes a non-ASCII host, so deleting the IDN.toASCII branch or replacing it with a pass-through leaves the suite green. The javadoc argues the step is unreachable through HTTP (java.net.URI returns a null host for a unicode authority) and says the step exists 'so the guarantee does not depend on that' - which is precisely a guarantee nothing currently checks.

findings.suggestion: Add a unit test DenylistThreatCheckTest against a stub ThreatDenylistRepository that lists nothing: aHostThatCannotBeCanonicalisedIsBlocked, asserting verdict(URI.create("http://4294967296/")) == BLOCK even with an empty denylist (so the mock cannot be what produces the answer), plus aCanonicalisedHostIsMatchedAgainstTheDenylist asserting the trailing-dot form of a listed row matches while notmalware.example.com does not.
findings.summary: Unpinned behaviour, cited at the implementation because no test file covers it: DenylistThreatCheck now returns BLOCK when the host cannot be canonicalised. That branch is unobservable over HTTP because UrlValidator.requireShortenable refuses the same host with 422 first, and there is no unit test for DenylistThreatCheck anywhere in the suite. Deleting the three lines would fail nothing. The code comment states the reason it exists - 'a security property that holds only because they run in a particular order is one reordering away from not holding' - and that is exactly the property that is currently unheld by any test: reorder the two checks and the suite stays green.

findings.suggestion: Add HostEvasionRefusalTest.aPublicAddressLiteralIsStillShortenable: POST a target with host 93.184.216.34, assert 201, assert longUrl comes back byte-identical, and assert a click sends Location to the submitted URL. Adding the URL to LOOKALIKE_URLS_STILL_ACCEPTED also makes hostsThatMerelyResembleARefusedOneAreStillShortened cover it, and makes theAnonymousPathAcceptsNoTargetTheAuthenticatedPathRefuses compare it on both paths.
findings.summary: The accept side of host normalisation is only exercised with registered names. LOOKALIKE_URLS_STILL_ACCEPTED holds two hostnames, and every URL in the suite whose host is numeric (Fixtures 327-368) is one that must be refused. So no test asserts that an ordinary public address literal - https://93.184.216.34/x - is still shortenable. An implementation that failed closed on any host the normaliser rewrote, or that treated every IPv4 candidate as internal, would pass all seventeen AC1/AC2 behaviours and silently stop existing customers shortening IP-literal targets, which is the over-refusal failure impact.json and the design both nominate as the most dangerous one here. The residual risk is smaller than it first looks (the unit tests show the numeric parser returns 127.0.0.1 for 127.0.0.1, and isInternal is unchanged), but the wiring assertion is absent.

findings.suggestion: Add SignUpTest.theEmailMaximumLengthIsInclusiveAndAnythingAboveItIsRefused, in the shape of the password pair: a 320-character address signs up with 201 and can then sign in; 321 characters answers 400 invalid_request with fields.email and leaves storedAccountsNamed empty.
findings.summary: SignUpRequest declares @Size(max = 320) on email and nothing tests either side of it. The password boundaries are pinned twice over (thePasswordMinimumLengthIsInclusiveAndAnythingBelowItIsRefused, thePasswordMaximumLengthIsInclusiveAndAnythingAboveItIsRefused, each asserting the fixture really sits on the boundary), so the omission is asymmetric rather than a house convention. An address ceiling that was dropped, or set to the wrong number, would be found by nothing - and the column width is what it is protecting.

findings.suggestion: In anonymousCreationIsRefusedWithTheExistingErrorWhileADependencyIsUnavailable, assert that at least one of the three attempts answered 503 - the create path needs invalidateBeforeIssuing and that cannot be done with the tier paused - keeping the existing per-response envelope assertions. If the run shows creation legitimately survives, say so in the javadoc rather than leaving the reader to infer that the branch was checked.
findings.summary: AC15's refusal half is asserted only conditionally, so it may never be exercised. Every claim about the 503 envelope is guarded - allMatch(201 || 503), then filter(statusCode != 201), then filter(statusCode == 503) - so an implementation whose anonymous create survives the Redis outage passes this class with the service_unavailable code, the catalogue message and the 'refused with the existing error response' sentence of AC15 never checked. Per the design the pre-issue cache invalidation makes the 503 deterministic when the shared tier is paused, so the tolerance may be wider than the implementation needs. I note this is the existing house pattern (DegradedDependencyTest.degradationIsSpentOnAcceptingLinksRatherThanOnServingClicks is written identically), so it is a consistency judgement rather than a defect introduced here.

findings.suggestion: Pin the assumption on the class: @SpringBootTest(properties = Fixtures.ANONYMOUS_CREATE_LIMIT_KEY + "=1000") on AnonymousLinkCreationTest, with a javadoc line saying the class needs the limit not to be reached and that throttling is AnonymousCreateRateLimitTest's subject - the same sentence the @BeforeEach already makes about bucket state.
findings.summary: theAnonymousPathAcceptsNoTargetTheAuthenticatedPathRefuses issues 25 anonymous creates in one method (11 + 5 + 2 + 7 fixtures), and the bucket is charged in PublicLinkController before validation, so all 25 spend a token. The class declares no properties, so it runs against the production default of app.rate-limit.anonymous-create-per-minute, which this change sets to 30: five requests of headroom, undeclared. The design explicitly invites an operator to lower it ('An operator who wants 10 changes one number'), and adding two fixtures to any of the three lists has the same effect. Every other class that depends on a bucket size pins it (AnonymousCreateRateLimitTest, SignUpRateLimitTest, WriteRateLimitTest); this one depends on it without saying so, and would fail as a mismatch between the two paths' status codes rather than as anything readable.

findings.suggestion: Sleep a quarter of the TTL rather than half, or compute the wait from link.expiresAt() rather than from the constant (e.g. wait until halfway between Instant.now() and expiresAt), so the margin shrinks with the round trip instead of being fixed. Keep the halfWay guard assertion either way.
findings.summary: Timing margin: anAnonymousLinkRedirectsUntilItsExpiryPasses runs against a 3-second anonymous TTL, sleeps half of it, and then needs the second click to complete before the link expires. Two HTTP round trips plus first-call warm-up have to fit in the remaining ~1.5s. It does fail loudly rather than silently - assertTrue(halfWay.isBefore(link.expiresAt())) is there precisely to say the wall clock was the cause - but on a loaded CI box this is the shape of test that gets muted, and a muted expiry test takes AC10 with it. Nothing else in the class has this problem: the other methods wait past the expiry rather than racing it.

findings.suggestion: No test change. Before AC3 is signed, a human should be shown the recorded failing run of HostEvasionRefusalTest against the pre-change commit (or an explicit statement that the ordering was not observed), since no artifact in this run demonstrates it and no test can.
findings.summary: AC3 has two halves and only one is met inside the repository. The tests that fail against the pre-change code do exist and would genuinely have failed (aDenylistedHostWithATrailingDotIsRefusedIdenticallyToTheHostItself and anInternalAddressWrittenAsOneDecimalNumberIsRefusedIdenticallyToTheDottedForm both returned 201 against the old UrlValidator and the old raw-host denylist walk), and they are retained. But AC3 also requires that failure to have been produced and visible before the fix, and plan.json T1 lists 'run log entry recording the failing run against pre-change code' as a deliverable: nothing under artifacts/ records a red run, and the pipeline's verify node runs after join, i.e. only ever against the fixed code. The test javadoc says as much - 'the before-and-after evidence is the run record, not a method here' - so the evidence has to come from outside the suite, and I could not find it.

not_examined: I did not run the suite. No verify artifact exists for this run (the verify node sits after join in sdlc.yaml and has not produced one), and I did not invoke Maven, so nothing here is backed by an observed pass, fail or timing. All judgements are from reading the assertions.

The 21 test classes inherited from before this change were read only where they bear on the new behaviour: I checked which endpoints they assert 401 for with no credential (confirming the session-filter exemption risk in impact.json is covered for POST/GET/PATCH/DELETE on /api/v1/links and for abuse reports) and read DegradedDependencyTest in full for comparison with AnonymousCreateDegradationTest. Their own adequacy was not reviewed.

TestInfrastructure.java was not read. I took withCounterTierUnavailable, resumeCounterTier and springProperties at face value from their call sites and from the existing degradation tests that already depend on them.

I did not verify that the new tests compile, nor that the four distinct @SpringBootTest property sets produce the intended separate cached contexts against shared containers. Cross-context interference through the single shared Redis is argued for in every new class's @BeforeEach javadoc; I could not confirm the argument holds at runtime.

Flakiness under CI load is not something reading can settle. TEST-7 is the one case where the margin looked small enough to name; there may be others in the click-flush waits (10.5s per assertion in AnonymousLinkRedirectTest) and the 60-second observeUntil polls that only a few real runs would expose.

artifacts/openapi.yaml was not cross-checked operation by operation against the tests - whether every documented response code has a test is the api-contract lens's question, and I answered only the narrower one of whether each acceptance criterion has a test.

The two migrations were read but not executed. Whether V3's unique index applies cleanly is untestable from this repository (only the two seeded rows exist), which SeededAccountsSurviveTest states rather than resolves; the duplicate-check result that has to accompany the approval is outside the suite.
summary: Unusually strong. Every acceptance criterion AC1-AC16 maps to at least one behaviour-named test that would fail if the behaviour were reverted, and the levels are chosen well: the equivalent-form filter is pinned both as a unit contract on HostNormalizer.normalize (where the many cases can be enumerated cheaply, including the rows that must NOT change) and as black-box HTTP refusals on POST /api/v1/links and POST /api/v1/public/links (where the wiring bug would live), and the two cannot disagree because both quote Fixtures. The behaviours no response can show are read from storage rather than asserted by proxy - AC6 through CustomerRepository, AC7 through the frozen PasswordHasher (comparing algorithm-and-parameters against a seeded row, not merely "not the plaintext"), AC13's ownerless row and AC11's click count through SQL, each with a javadoc justifying the exception. AC6's concurrent case uses a released latch rather than a loop, which is the only arrangement that can distinguish a read-then-write from a constraint. Failure paths are covered rather than skipped: malformed and missing fields, unknown properties, both password boundaries, the 2048-character URL boundary on both sides, expired, blocked, unissued, somebody else's and nobody's all asserted byte-identical, 429 with a non-zero whole-second Retry-After, 503 envelopes, and 405 (not 401) on the other verbs of the two newly exempted paths. No existing test file was modified - the only change under src/test outside new files is additive helpers on AbstractIntegrationTest - so AC17 is not being bought by weakening anything. The "extra assertion bolted onto an existing test" failure mode is essentially absent: fourteen new classes, one behaviour family each, and the assertions that ride along (the Location on a redirect test, the credential check inside the sign-in test) are about the behaviour they sit in. My eight findings are all minor and none of them is a missing acceptance criterion: three are unpinned defence-in-depth branches the contract specified and nothing checks (HostNormalizer's IDN step, DenylistThreatCheck's fail-closed path), one is a missing accept-side fixture for numeric hosts, one a missing email-length boundary, and three are robustness or evidence concerns (an undeclared dependency on a production rate-limit default, a 1.5-second timing margin, and the absent record of AC3's red run).
